title: What a Lifetime Shingle Warranty Covers
description: Lifetime usually means as long as you own the house, on the material, often prorated, and not for hail. Workmanship is a separate piece of paper.
html:
The bundle says lifetime. The homeowner hears “if anything happens, it is free.” The warranty says something narrower, in smaller type, and the gap between those two readings is where arguments start.

What the shingle maker is promising

On most architectural shingles, “lifetime” means the material warranty lasts as long as you own the home, sometimes with a transfer if you sell, sometimes with a shorter term for the next owner. Defects in the shingle itself are covered. The coverage is often full for a set number of years and prorated after that, so a claim in year twenty pays a fraction of the material. Labor to tear off and reinstall may be included only in the early years, or not at all.

Hail, wind above a stated speed, and hurricanes are commonly excluded or limited. A bruise from last April is an insurance question or a repair bill, not a call to the shingle plant. So is a leak from a boot the crew installed wrong. That second one is workmanship.

Workmanship is our paper, not theirs

The manufacturer did not flash your chimney. We did. Our workmanship warranty covers the installation. Theirs covers the shingle. You want both, in writing, before the tear-off starts, with the length and what is excluded. If a bid will not put that on a page, the word lifetime on the shingle wrapper is doing all the selling.

Keep the paperwork with the house

The warranty is only as good as the proof: the shingle name, the color, the date, the contractor, and whether the maker registered an enhanced warranty because a certified crew installed it. Put that packet with the closing papers. The next owner, and the next storm, will ask for it. A wrapper in a garage trash can is not a warranty.
